messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 71

He is a 56-year-old European man who has spent most of his life around music, and for years he thought of himself as someone who could read a room, hold a stage, and stay composed no matter what was happening inside. The assault occurs in his early adulthood, after a night that begins like so many others in his world of performances, late conversations, and drinking after a show. He trusts someone he knows. The details still come to him in fragments rather than as a clean sequence: a sudden shift in tone, the realization that his body is not being treated as his own, the humiliating sense that he cannot make the moment stop. What stays with him most is not only the violence of it, but the shock of betrayal and the silence that follows. He tells himself afterward that he should be able to push through, that a man in his world cannot afford to fall apart. He keeps moving, keeps playing, keeps smiling when expected.

In the years that follow, he builds a life that looks steady from the outside. He marries. He continues working as a musician, performing in venues where people expect him to be confident, relaxed, even charismatic. Onstage, he can sometimes disappear into the structure of a song. The rhythm gives him a place to stand. Offstage, he is more guarded. He starts sitting near exits in restaurants, checking locks, and becoming tense when someone comes up behind him without warning. Intimacy with his wife is complicated by a body that does not always feel like it belongs to him. At times he pulls away without knowing how to explain why, ashamed of the distance even as he creates it. He does not talk about what happened. For many years he experiences the assault as something sealed away, but it leaks into daily life through irritability, sleep that is light and easily broken, and a constant watchfulness that he mistakes for prudence.

As he gets older, the memories become harder to keep contained. Certain sounds, smells, and settings seem to catch on the trauma and bring it back with force. A crowded backstage area, a particular perfume, a hand on his shoulder from the wrong angle—these can set off a surge of nausea, heat, and a feeling that he is suddenly no longer in the present. He finds himself looking over his shoulder in places that should be familiar. At night he lies awake replaying scenes in his mind, not because he wants to but because they arrive with their own momentum. Sometimes the images are vivid and intrusive; other times he feels only the bodily echo of them: tight chest, clenched jaw, shallow breathing. He wakes from dreams drenched in sweat, embarrassed by how quickly his heart races, as if his body has not learned that the event is long over.

He notices that he has narrowed his life in small ways. He declines certain gigs if they involve travel alone. He avoids conversations that might drift toward sexual topics or vulnerability. He drinks less than he once did, partly because alcohol makes the memories less containable. When he is overwhelmed, he becomes quiet and distant, present in the room but not fully reachable. His wife knows him as loving but often self-protective, and she has learned not to push too hard when he seems to retreat into himself. He feels guilt about this distance and shame that, even after all these years, one act committed against him still has the power to shape his days.

In sessions, he speaks with the carefulness of someone who has spent decades editing his own story. He does not tell it all at once. He circles around it, testing whether it can be spoken aloud without collapsing him. What emerges is a man who has carried terror and humiliation for most of his adult life, hidden beneath competence and routine. He still works, still shows up, still knows how to make a room listen when he plays. But he now describes his inner life as organized around anticipation of danger, as if some part of him remains stationed at the moment before the assault, waiting for the world to turn again.
